summary: Adds a Connection ID (CID) to DTLS 1.2. Normally a DTLS receiver identifies a session by the sender's address and port, which breaks if those change mid-session, for example after a network switch or a NAT rebinding. With a CID in the record header, the receiver can still find the right security context. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: DTLS normally finds a session by the address and port that data came from, so a session breaks when a router or NAT changes that address. This RFC adds a short identifier to every encrypted record, so the receiver can find the session even when the address has moved.

questions: dtls session after ip address change
how does cid work in dtls 1.2
subtitle: A connection identifier in the DTLS 1.2 record header, so a session survives a change of IP address or port.

tldr.problem: DTLS 1.2 finds the right security context from the sender's address and port. If the source address or port changes during a session, for example after a NAT rebinding, the receiver cannot find the session and a costly new handshake is needed.
tldr.mechanism: Both sides negotiate a connection_id extension in the hello messages. Afterwards each encrypted record carries the CID the receiver asked for, in a new record format with content type tls12_cid(25), a changed MAC computation, an encrypted real content type and optional padding.
tldr.outcome: The receiver can look up the session by CID, while strict rules on peer address updates limit spoofing and replay. The RFC warns that a persistent identifier adds linkability, and recommends DTLS 1.3 where the identifier can be changed.

today: RFC 9146 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2022. It updates RFC 6347 and is itself updated by RFC 9853. The text points to a separate DTLS 1.3 specification for carrying a CID in DTLS 1.3 and recommends moving to that version where a CID can be updated.

sections.title: Why DTLS Needs a Connection ID
sections.content:
Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS), defined in RFC 6347, protects data sent over datagram transports such as UDP. Like TLS, it starts with a handshake that can be expensive, particularly when public key cryptography is used. After the handshake, symmetric key cryptography protects the data, and the second phase should last as long as possible so that the handshake cost is spread over many packets.

In DTLS as specified in RFC 6347, the IP address and port of the peer identify the DTLS association. In some cases those values are not enough. A NAT rebinding is the clearest example: the address changes and the connection fails, and the price is a new handshake. This matters most in the Internet of Things, where devices sleep for long periods to save battery and so are more likely to see their address change.

This RFC therefore adds a Connection ID (CID) to the DTLS record layer, negotiated through a DTLS extension. Adding a CID to the ciphertext record format also opens the door to other changes, and this RFC takes two of them from TLS 1.3: the real record type is encrypted, and a padding mechanism lets a sender hide the length of the plaintext.
sections.plainLanguage: DTLS labels a session by the address and port the data comes from. When a NAT changes that address, the session is lost and the two ends have to shake hands again. A short identifier in each record solves that.

sections.title: The connection_id Extension
sections.content:
The connection_id extension, type 54, is carried in the ClientHello and the ServerHello. In the ClientHello the extension data must contain the ConnectionId structure, an opaque value of up to 255 bytes, and it holds the CID the client wants the server to use when sending to the client. A zero-length value means the client is willing to send using a CID but does not want the server to use one.

A server willing to use CIDs answers with a connection_id extension in the ServerHello holding the CID it wants the client to use when sending to it. A zero-length value means the server will send using the client's CID but does not want the client to include one.

Because each side sends the value it wants to receive, a deployment can fix the length of the CIDs it uses, which makes parsing and connection lookup easier. Implementations must still be able to send CIDs of different lengths to other parties, and since the record itself does not say how long the CID is, an implementation that uses variable-length CIDs must build them so that their length can be worked out on arrival.

In DTLS 1.2 the CIDs are exchanged only at the start of a session. There is no message for changing a CID in the middle of a session, because DTLS 1.2 does not allow TLS 1.3 style post-handshake messages that do not themselves start another handshake. A resumed or renegotiated session negotiates the extension afresh.
sections.plainLanguage: Each side says which identifier it wants to receive, and the other side puts that identifier on the records it sends. The length can be fixed by configuration, which makes it easy to look up the session.

sections.title: The CID-Enhanced Record Format
sections.content:
Connections that have negotiated the extension use a distinguished record type, tls12_cid(25), so the receiver can tell at once whether a record carries a CID. When that content type is set, the CID field is present with one or more bytes, the MAC follows the calculation in Section 5, and the real content type is inside the encryption envelope.

The plaintext structure is unchanged. The content to be sent is first wrapped, together with its real content type and optional padding, into a new DTLSInnerPlaintext structure with three parts: the content, the real type describing the cleartext payload, and a run of zero bytes used as padding. The padding lets a sender pad any record by a chosen amount as long as the total stays within the record size limits, which hides the length of the plaintext from an observer.

The DTLSInnerPlaintext is then encrypted, and the CID is added to make the DTLSCiphertext structure. Its outer type is always tls12_cid, and the new cid field holds the CID value, of the length agreed during the handshake. The real content type is found in the real_type field after decryption. All other fields are as defined in RFC 6347. When the peers have not negotiated a CID, or a zero-length CID was agreed for a direction, the record format of RFC 6347 must be used in that direction, and plaintext payloads never use the new format or the new content type.
sections.plainLanguage: Encrypted records that carry a CID get a new marker, a new field for the identifier, and an encrypted record type. The sender can also add padding so that the length of the message is not visible.

sections.title: Record Payload Protection
sections.content:
The MAC calculation changes for records with the content type tls12_cid, and the modified algorithm must not be applied to records without a CID. The construction keeps the two cases apart: a record without a CID is covered by a sequence number followed by some other content type, while a record with a CID is covered by a placeholder of eight bytes of 0xff followed by tls12_cid. Since tls12_cid is never a valid content type when the CID is not in use, the two MAC inputs can never be confused. The epoch and the sequence number now enter the MAC in the same order as they appear on the wire.

Three variants are given. For block ciphers that do not use Encrypt-then-MAC, the MAC covers the placeholder, the content type, the CID length, the version, the epoch, the sequence number, the CID, the length of the inner plaintext, and then the content, the real type and the padding. For block ciphers that do use Encrypt-then-MAC, the MAC covers the same fields but with the ciphertext length and the encrypted content instead. For AEAD ciphers, the same fields form the additional data. The length of the serialized inner plaintext is a two-byte integer and must not exceed 2^14.
sections.plainLanguage: The way the record is signed changes so that the identifier is covered by the signature, and so that a record with an identifier can never be mistaken for one without.

sections.title: Updating the Peer Address
sections.content:
When a record with a CID arrives from an address other than the one currently associated with the DTLS connection, the receiver must not start sending to that new address unless three conditions are met. The datagram must have been cryptographically verified using the record layer procedures. It must be newer, in both epoch and sequence number, than the newest datagram received, because a reordered datagram from before an address change could otherwise revert a valid change, and because this limits what an attacker can do with replayed datagrams. And there must be a strategy for making sure the new address can receive and process DTLS records; no strategy is mandated, but the RFC points to a return routability check.

Datagrams that pass the cryptographic checks but do not cause an address change are still valid records and must still be passed to the application. DTLS implementations must silently discard records with bad MACs or that are otherwise invalid.
sections.plainLanguage: A session may follow its peer to a new address, but only when the record is correctly signed, is newer than anything seen before, and there is a plan for reaching the new address.

sections.title: Example Exchange
sections.content:
The RFC's example shows a CID used in one direction only, from the client to the server. The client sends a ClientHello with a zero-length connection_id, receives a HelloVerifyRequest with a cookie, and repeats the ClientHello with the cookie. The server's ServerHello carries connection_id=100, and the server's other handshake messages follow. The client's Finished message and its application data then carry the CID 100 in the record layer, while the server's application data uses the ordinary record format.

The example also shows when the CID appears. In DTLS 1.2 only one handshake message is encrypted, the Finished message, so the CID is only on the records that carry the Finished message or application data.
sections.plainLanguage: In the example, the client asks to receive the identifier 100 and then puts that identifier on the records it sends. The server keeps using the ordinary format.

sections.title: Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
The CID replaces the 5-tuple, and it stays the same for the life of the DTLS connection. Every identifier carries a risk of linkability, as explained in RFC 6973. An on-path observer can link the payloads it sees to all later payloads that carry the same pair of identifiers. Without multihoming or mobility, the CID exposes the same information as the 5-tuple did.

With multihoming, a passive attacker can correlate the communication over the two paths, and because DTLS 1.2 has no way to update a CID, this extension is unsuitable for mobility situations where correlation matters. A deployment that uses DTLS with multihoming and cares about this should refuse to use CIDs in DTLS 1.2 and move to DTLS 1.3, where a CID update mechanism and sequence number encryption are available.

Padding is a privacy feature that the original DTLS 1.2 did not have, because it lets a sender inflate the ciphertext and make traffic analysis harder. Endpoints can also attach arbitrary per-connection metadata to the records they receive, which may leak information to on-path observers, and implementations worried about that should refuse to use CIDs.
sections.plainLanguage: A CID stays the same for the whole session, so anyone watching the network can tell that two packets belong to the same conversation. Padding hides the size of messages, but the identifier itself is a lasting mark.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
An on-path adversary can mount reflection attacks against third parties, because a DTLS peer has no way to tell a genuine address update, such as one caused by a NAT rebinding, from a malicious one. The attack is worst when the request is small and the response is large. An attacker who can observe the traffic between two DTLS peers can also replay datagrams with modified IP addresses and port numbers.

Both problems are addressed by the rules on peer address updates in Section 6: an address change has to be backed by a cryptographically verified, newer datagram, so a replayed or spoofed datagram cannot move the session to an address of the attacker's choosing.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone on the path could try to move the session to an address they control. The rules about when an address change is allowed are what stop that, and they also stop replayed packets from doing it.
